EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN – “PNTR, Chinese Import Competition, and U.S. Manufacturing Employment, 1990-2007”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Primary strategy: Difference-in-Differences with staggered intensity (“Bartik-style” continuous DiD) complemented by an IV that uses the pre-PNTR “NTR-gap” as an exogenous shifter of post-2001 Chinese import growth.

Why it fits
• Treatment is a policy shock (PNTR, October 2000) common to all industries but whose bite differs predictably with pre-policy exposure to China.  
• We observe a long pre- and post-period, allowing pre-trend tests and an event-study.  
• The NTR-gap—difference between the higher Smoot–Hawley (column 2) tariff and the MFN tariff—creates exogenous cross-industry variation in the size of the policy shock (Handley & Limão, 2017).  
• Combining DiD with the IV removes endogeneity of realized import growth to contemporaneous industry shocks.

Formal model (first stage continuous DiD):
ΔImports_{it} = α_i + γ_t + θ(Post_t × NTRgap_i) + ε_{it}

Second stage:
Employment_{it} = α_i + γ_t + β × ŶΔImports_{it} + X'_{it}δ + u_{it}

β is the causal semi-elasticity of employment with respect to PNTR-induced Chinese import penetration.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment intensity:  
TREAT_i = NTR Gap_i  (pre-PNTR tariff uncertainty, measured in 1999).

Timing:  
POST_t = 1 {t ≥ 2001} (first full calendar year after Congressional approval).

Binary illustration (for graphs only): “High-exposure” = top quartile of NTR-gap, “Low-exposure” = bottom quartile.

Counterfactual: Industries with low (near-zero) NTR-gap that faced little change in tariff uncertainty.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends: Absent PNTR, high- and low-gap industries would have followed similar employment paths.  
 Plausibility: We can visually and formally test in 1990-1999 data; pre-PNTR gap has no predictive power for trends in the 1990s.

A2. Exogeneity of NTR-gap: Differences in statutory vs. MFN tariffs were fixed in the 1930s and unrelated to 1990s/2000s industry-specific shocks.  
 Plausible given historical tariff codification; we will control for observables (capital intensity, skill mix) to bolster.

A3. No anticipation: Firms did not adjust employment materially before 2000 in response to rumors of PNTR.  
 Reasonable—PNTR approval was uncertain until votes in mid-2000.

A4. Stable Unit Treatment Value (no spillovers across industries).  
 Potentially problematic (input-output linkages). We will verify robustness excluding supplier industries and clustering at 4-digit industry × year.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Differential pre-trends or contemporaneous shocks (e.g., Dot-com bust).  
 • Event-study coefficients for −10…−1 years.  
 • Include industry-specific linear pre-trends.  
 • Test placebo “fake PNTR” in 1995.

T2. Offshoring or outsourcing to non-China locations simultaneously correlated with NTR-gap.  
 • Add control: import growth from non-China low-wage countries.  
 • Falsification: use NTR-gap to predict EU import growth—they should not covary strongly.

T3. Measurement error in Chinese imports at 4-digit level.  
 • Instrumental-variables framework already mitigates attenuation.  
 • Aggregate to 3-digit and check robustness.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# PACKAGES ----------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast high-dimensional FE
library(modelsummary)

# DATA --------------------------------------------------------------
# Assume two csv files: lbd.csv and nber_ces.csv already harmonised by indyear
lbd  <- fread("lbd.csv")          # has employment
nber <- fread("nber_ces.csv")     # has import flows, output etc.

# Merge
dt <- merge(lbd, nber, by = c("naics4", "year"))

# VARIABLE CONSTRUCTION --------------------------------------------
dt[, Post      := as.integer(year >= 2001)]
dt[, NTRgap    := ntr_gap_1999]                       # fixed
dt[, Treat_int := Post * NTRgap]                      # DiD interaction

# Outcome levels and logs
dt[, ln_emp := log(1 + employment)]
dt[, imp_penetration := chinese_imports / shipments]  # imports over output

# FIRST STAGE (continuous DiD) -----------------------
fs <- feols(imp_penetration ~ Treat_int | naics4 + year,
            data = dt, weights = dt$employment_base)
summary(fs)

# SECOND STAGE IV -----------------------------------
ss <- feols(ln_emp ~ 1 | naics4 + year | imp_penetration ~ Treat_int ,
            data = dt, weights = dt$employment_base,
            cluster = ~naics4)
etable(fs, ss)

# EVENT STUDY ROBUSTNESS -----------------------------
es <- feols(
  ln_emp ~ sunab(Post, NTRgap) | naics4 + year,
  data = dt, weights = dt$employment_base, cluster = ~naics4)
iplot(es, ref.line = 0)

# PRE-TREND TEST -------------------------------------
pretrend <- feols(ln_emp ~ NTRgap:factor(year) | naics4 + year,
                  data = dt[year <= 1999])
wald(pretrend, keep = "NTRgap:")
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Economic priors and past literature (e.g., Pierce & Schott 2016) suggest a sizeable negative effect.  
Ballpark: A one-standard-deviation larger NTR-gap (~7 pp) should lower manufacturing employment by roughly 10–15 percent cumulatively by 2007, i.e., β ≈ −0.015 log-points per 1 pp import-penetration increase.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (Diff-in-Diff)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1. Credible parallel pre-trends ............. 0.8  
C2. Policy timing exogenous/ sharp ........... 1  
C3. No interference across units ............. 0.5  
C4. Treatment stable and accurately measured .. 0.9  
C5. Robust standard errors / correct inference 1  

Total ≈ 4.2 / 5.  Main weakness: possible cross-industry spillovers.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
End of Plan
